metadata.title: What Fine-Tuning a Language Model Actually Changes

beats.narration_text: Fine-tuning gets described as teaching a model new facts. It mostly isn't. It is a decision about how much of the model you are willing to move. I'm Anjana.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself

props.command: I keep being told to fine-tune a model on my own data, and I cannot tell what that would actually change inside it. Does it learn new facts? Does it forget what it already knew? And do I have to retrain the whole thing, or is there a version of this that fits on one machine?
output: it moves weights; it does not file away new facts
how much of it moves is the thing you choose
and the smallest useful move is under one percent

beats.narration_text: Before any fine-tuning happens, a pre-trained language model already knows a lot. Billions of parameters trained on broad internet text encode grammar in the lower layers, facts and semantics in the middle layers, and higher-level reasoning patterns in the upper layers. It can write, summarize, and answer questions out of the box. But it speaks general English. It doesn't know that "guidance" in a corporate context means a forward-looking earnings estimate, not directions to a destination. The knowledge is broad but not deep in any one domain.

Continued pre-training fixes that. You take the pre-trained model and keep training it — same objective, masked language modeling — but on your domain's text. Financial transcripts, whatever your field produces. Every layer updates. The model's internal associations shift. Words that had generic meanings develop domain-specific weight. The statistical patterns of how experts in your field write — sentence structure, terminology, common phrasings — get absorbed into the model's representations. It still knows general English, but now it speaks your language natively.

Task-specific fine-tuning is different. Instead of learning a domain's language broadly, you teach the model to do one thing well. You add a small task head on top — a classifier, a regressor, whatever your task needs — and train on labeled examples. Text paired with the correct output. Gradients flow backward from the task head through the upper layers, adjusting the representations to serve that specific task. Lower layers change less because syntax and grammar are already useful as they are. The model doesn't learn a new language. It learns a new skill.

props.sparkLine: A new skill, not a new language.

beats.narration_text: Full fine-tuning updates every parameter. For a seven-billion-parameter model, that's expensive — you need to store gradients and optimizer states for all of them. Parameter-efficient methods skip that. LoRA freezes the original weights entirely and inserts small trainable adapter matrices beside a few key layers. Instead of updating seven billion parameters, you train maybe ten million — a fraction of a percent. The adapters learn a small adjustment on top of the frozen weights. The result is nearly as good as full fine-tuning at a fraction of the memory and compute cost. QLoRA goes further by quantizing the frozen weights to four bits, shrinking the memory footprint even more.

props.sparkLine: Freeze it all, train a patch.

beats.act: WHEN DOMAIN DATA BEATS MODEL SIZE
beats.narration_text: Here's the practical takeaway. On domain-specific tasks, a smaller model fine-tuned on domain data often outperforms a much larger general-purpose model. A seven-billion-parameter model that's seen thousands of financial transcripts understands corporate language better than a seventy-billion-parameter model that hasn't. Scale helps, but domain knowledge compounds. The model that speaks your language, even if it's smaller, usually gives you better answers than the model that speaks every language equally. Fine-tuning isn't just an optimization. It's how you make the model yours.

props.sparkLine: Smaller, but it has read your documents.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Fine-tuning is one question asked three ways: how much of the model are you willing to move? Pre-training already did the general work, so the answer is usually less than people expect. Continued pre-training moves every layer, and what comes back is a model that speaks your field's dialect rather than general English. Task fine-tuning moves the top and leaves the grammar alone, because the grammar was already fine. And a parameter-efficient adapter moves none of the original weights at all — it freezes them and trains a patch beside them, about a seventh of a percent of the parameter count. The last beat is the one worth remembering: a small model that has read your documents will beat a large one that has not.

lines: pre-training already did the general work
task tuning moves the top and leaves the grammar
an adapter moves none of it and trains beside it
and the small tuned model beats the big general one

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Before you fine-tune anything, work out which of the three you actually need — the whole model moved, the top of it moved. Paste this into Claude with a description of your task and the data you have, and ask it to argue you down to the smallest of the three that would still solve your problem.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Your turn.'; prompt types itself

props.command: I am considering fine-tuning a language model. Can you help me work out which of three things I actually need: one, continued pre-training, where every layer moves and the model learns my field's language — and whether I have enough unlabelled domain text for that to mean anything; two, task fine-tuning, where I add a head and move the upper layers, which needs labelled examples I may not have; or three, a parameter-efficient adapter that freezes the original weights and trains well under a percent of them. Argue me down to the smallest of the three that would still solve my problem, and tell me what evidence would change your answer.
